lessons.title: Mappings and function notation
lessons.summary: Classify mappings and use the notation of functions with confidence.
lessons.objective: Classify mappings and use the notation of functions with confidence.
lessons.before: Read the inputs first. A function assigns exactly one output to every permitted input.
lessons.ideas:
Two arrows may arrive at one output. Two different outputs from a single input break the function rule.

\(f(3)\) means apply the rule at input \(3\).

A one-to-one function has one input for each output in its range.
lessons.method:
What makes a rule a function?

Read the inputs first. A function assigns exactly one output to every permitted input.

How do I use function notation?

Read the bracket as an instruction about the input. Replace the input wherever it occurs in the rule.

When is a function one-to-one?

Compare outputs for different inputs. If at least two distinct inputs give the same output, it is many-to-one.
mistakes: A repeated output does not on its own make a relation invalid.
Do not multiply the name of the function by its input.
Check where arrows end, as well as where they start.

examples.title: Read a mapping and explain its type
examples.question:
The table shows a relation from the input values to the output values.

InputOutput
\(2\)\(-1\)
\(5\)\(5\)
\(2\)\(8\)

Which description fits this rule?

A. A one-to-one function B. A many-to-one function C. A relation that is not a function
examples.solution:
Check how many outputs belong to each input first, then look for shared outputs.

The input \(2\) has the two different outputs \(-1\) and \(8\).

Final answer: A relation that is not a function.

examples.title: Use function notation to identify values
examples.question:
A function is defined by \(f:x\mapsto 3 \left(x - 2\right)^{2} + 2\) for all real \(x\).

Find \(f(1)\).
examples.solution:
Replace every occurrence of the input by the named value.

Subtract \(2\) within the brackets before squaring, then multiply and add.

Final answer: \(5\).

examples.title: Read a mapping and explain its type
examples.question:
The input and output pairs for a rule are shown in the table.

InputOutput
\(3\)\(-3\)
\(9\)\(9\)
\(15\)\(-3\)

Which description fits this rule?

A. A one-to-one function B. A many-to-one function C. A relation that is not a function
examples.solution:
Check how many outputs belong to each input first, then look for shared outputs.

Every listed input has exactly one output. The first and last inputs both give \(-3\).

Final answer: A many-to-one function.

lessons.title: Domain and range
lessons.summary: Find the complete set of legal inputs and outputs for square-root and reciprocal functions.
lessons.objective: Find the complete set of legal inputs and outputs for square-root and reciprocal functions.
lessons.before: Locate the expression underneath the root sign. Its value must be at least zero.
lessons.ideas:
Include the zero endpoint of a square root when nothing else excludes it.

A square-root term subtracted from a constant gives a maximum output at the start of the domain.

A non-zero constant divided by a finite non-zero number never equals zero.
lessons.method:
Which inputs make a real square root?

Locate the expression underneath the root sign. Its value must be at least zero.

What changes when a square root is subtracted?

Track how its input changes from zero to large positive values. Multiplying a result by a negative number reverses its order.

Which input and output are missing from a reciprocal?

Check where the denominator is zero. Then ask which horizontal level the output approaches without reaching.
mistakes: A square root can equal zero. Use a closed endpoint in this case.
The minimum input need not give the minimum output.
Do not put the domain restriction on the output variable or vice versa.

examples.title: Find all allowed inputs and outputs
examples.question:
Consider the real-valued function \(f(x)=\sqrt{2 x - 2} - 2\) on its largest possible real domain.

State the domain of the function.
examples.solution:
Make the expression inside the square root non-negative.

The radicand is zero at the left endpoint, so the endpoint is included.

Final answer: \(x\ge 1\).

examples.title: Find all allowed inputs and outputs
examples.question:
Consider the real-valued function \(f(x)=2 - \sqrt{x - 2}\) on its largest possible real domain.

Find the range of the function.
examples.solution:
Use the limiting or extreme values of the output.

Subtracting a non-negative square-root value from \(2\) gives a maximum of \(2\).

Final answer: \(y\le 2\).

examples.title: Find all allowed inputs and outputs
examples.question:
Consider the real-valued function \(f(x)=-1 + \frac{5}{x - 3}\) on its largest possible real domain.

Find the range of the function.
examples.solution:
Use the limiting or extreme values of the output.

The fraction cannot equal zero. Solving \(y=-1 + \frac{5}{x - 3}\) for \(x\) gives a real input for every \(y\ne -1\) .

Final answer: \(y\ne -1\).

lessons.title: Composite functions and their domains
lessons.summary: Choose the right order, apply the inner rule and restrict its output when needed.
lessons.objective: Choose the right order, apply the inner rule and restrict its output when needed.
lessons.before: Think of two boxes connected in a row. The inner rule sees the original input. Its result is what enters the outer rule.
lessons.ideas:
\(fg(x)=f(g(x))\). Work from the bracket outwards.

\(f^2(x)=f(f(x))\) in this context.

Check both domains. Solve the condition that the first output fits the next rule's domain.
lessons.method:
Which rule goes first?

Think of two boxes connected in a row. The inner rule sees the original input. Its result is what enters the outer rule.

Does f squared mean the output is squared?

In the Cambridge composition notation the superscript on the function name indicates that the rule is applied twice.

How can one rule limit the next?

An initial input can be allowed by the inner rule while the first output is refused by the outer rule.
mistakes: Interchanging the two rules can give a different output.
Applying the same function twice is different from squaring a value.
For an inverse inequality, dividing by a negative coefficient reverses the order.

examples.title: Choose the correct order of a composition
examples.question:
Let \(f(x)=3 x + 1\) and \(g(x)=\left(x - 2\right)^{2}\).

Find an expression for \(fg(x)\).
examples.solution:
Apply the right-hand function first.

Substitute \(\left(x - 2\right)^{2}\) for the input of \(f\), then simplify.

Final answer: \(3 x^{2} - 12 x + 13\).

examples.title: Choose the correct order of a composition
examples.question:
Let \(f(x)=4 x + 2\) and \(g(x)=\left(x - 1\right)^{2}\).

Find \(f^2(x)\), where the superscript denotes composition.
examples.solution:
Use the output of the first application of f as a new input.

Substitute \(4 x + 2\) for x in \(f(x)\).

Final answer: \(16 x + 10\).

examples.title: Restrict a composite's domain
examples.question:
Let \(f(x)=\sqrt{x - 4}\) on its natural domain and \(g(x)=3 - 3 x\) for all real \(x\).

Find the domain of \(fg\).
examples.solution:
The output of g must be a valid input of f.

Solve \(3 - 3 x\ge 4\). Reverse the inequality when dividing by a negative number.

Final answer: \(x\le - \frac{1}{3}\).

lessons.title: Linear and quadratic modulus graphs
lessons.summary: Reflect negative outputs and preserve intercepts when sketching a modulus graph.
lessons.objective: Reflect negative outputs and preserve intercepts when sketching a modulus graph.
lessons.before: For each input, measure how far the original output lies from zero.
lessons.ideas:
Positive outputs stay where they are. Negative outputs reflect in the horizontal axis.

The corner of a linear modulus graph is at the zero of the original line.

A negative vertex becomes a positive peak between the same two roots.
lessons.method:
What does the modulus change?

For each input, measure how far the original output lies from zero.

Where do the rays meet?

Find the zero of the linear expression. That point belongs to both pieces of the absolute-value graph.

How can I sketch a quadratic's modulus?

Mark both original roots and the turning point. Identify which section was below the axis.
mistakes: The input is unchanged, including negative inputs.
Reflect only the ray below the axis.
Take the modulus of the y-intercept too if it is negative.

examples.title: Sketch the modulus of a graph
examples.question:
The function \(g\) is defined by \(g(x)=|2 x - 2|\).

Find \(g(-1)\).
examples.solution:
Evaluate the expression inside the modulus, then take its non-negative magnitude.

The value before taking the modulus is \(-4\).

Final answer: \(4\).

examples.title: Sketch the modulus of a graph
examples.question:
The function \(g\) is defined by \(g(x)=|2 x - 4|\).

Write the set containing every x-intercept.
examples.solution:
The modulus is zero exactly where its input is zero.

Solve \(2 x - 4=0\).

Final answer: \(\{2\}\).

examples.title: Sketch the modulus of a graph
examples.question:
The function \(g\) is defined by \(g(x)=|2 \left(x - 3\right)^{2} - 8|\).

Give the complete set of x-intercepts.
examples.solution:
Find the points where the quadratic is zero before taking its modulus.

Solve \((x-3)^2=4\). Both signs are needed.

Final answer: \(\{1, 5\}\).

lessons.title: Inverse functions and exact values
lessons.summary: Undo linear and reciprocal rules and verify answers by composing the two functions.
lessons.objective: Undo linear and reciprocal rules and verify answers by composing the two functions.
lessons.before: Write the original output as a new variable. Rearrange first, before giving the inverse its usual name.
lessons.ideas:
Undo operations in reverse order.

A restriction on the original range becomes a restriction on the inverse domain.

Look for \(f(f^{-1}(z))=z\) for a permitted input \(z\).
lessons.method:
How can I reverse a linear rule?

Write the original output as a new variable. Rearrange first, before giving the inverse its usual name.

How can I undo a reciprocal rule?

Move the output shift before multiplying by the denominator. This exposes the only prohibited inverse input.

How do I verify an inverse value?

Treat the proposed inverse result as an input of the original function. It must reproduce the given output.
mistakes: Dividing each term before moving an addition can give a wrong constant.
A reciprocal shift in the output changes the denominator of the inverse.
Check the value in the original rule as well as rearranging the symbols.

examples.title: Find and use an inverse function
examples.question:
Let \(f(x)=3 x + 1\), for real x.

Find \(f^{-1}(x)\).
examples.solution:
Swap input and output, then isolate the new output.

Undo addition of \(1\), then undo multiplication by \(3\).

Final answer: \(\frac{x}{3} - \frac{1}{3}\).

examples.title: Find and use an inverse function
examples.question:
Let \(f(x)=1 + \frac{3}{x - 2}\), \(x\ne 2\).

Give the value excluded from the domain of the inverse.
examples.solution:
Isolate the reciprocal term before switching the variable names.

From \(y=1 + \frac{3}{x - 2}\), multiply by \(x-2\) and divide by \(y-(1)\). The inverse excludes the original range gap. The inverse is \(f^{-1}(x)=2 + \frac{3}{x - 1}\).

Final answer: \(1\).

examples.title: Find and use an inverse function
examples.question:
Let \(f(x)=-4 + \frac{3}{x - 3}\), \(x\ne 3\).

Find \(f^{-1}(-1)\).
examples.solution:
Find the input that the original function sends to the given output.

Substitution confirms \(f(4)=-1\).

Final answer: \(4\).

lessons.title: Inverse branches of quadratic functions
lessons.summary: Select the correct branch and track the domain and range after reversal.
lessons.objective: Select the correct branch and track the domain and range after reversal.
lessons.before: A full parabola may return the same output twice. Restrict the original domain to one branch so that reversal is a function.
lessons.ideas:
The range of the restricted original is the inverse domain.

The inverse formula takes the positive square-root offset on the right-hand branch.

Use the negative square-root offset from the vertex on the left branch.
lessons.method:
Which domain will the inverse have?

A full parabola may return the same output twice. Restrict the original domain to one branch so that reversal is a function.

Which square root is valid on the right?

For inputs to the right of the vertex, the horizontal offset from its centre is non-negative.

What changes on the left-hand branch?

The horizontal offset is now non-positive. The output still gives a valid non-negative value under the square root.
mistakes: Include the vertex only when it belongs to the named branch.
The other algebraic root is outside the original domain.
Choose the sign from the original domain, regardless of the sign of the final input.

examples.title: Invert a quadratic on a single branch
examples.question:
The function \(f(x)=2 \left(x - 2\right)^{2} - 3\) has domain \(x\ge 2\).

State the domain of the inverse.
examples.solution:
The range of the original becomes the domain of its inverse.

The vertex gives the minimum output \(-3\) and it is included.

Final answer: \(x\ge -3\).

examples.title: Invert a quadratic on a single branch
examples.question:
The function \(f(x)=2 \left(x - 3\right)^{2} + 1\) has domain \(x\ge 3\).

Choose the full expression for \(f^{-1}(x)\).

A. \(3 - \sqrt{\frac{x}{2} - \frac{1}{2}}\) B. \(\sqrt{\frac{x}{2} + \frac{1}{2}} + 3\) C. \(\sqrt{\frac{x}{2} - \frac{1}{2}} + 3\)
examples.solution:
Rearrange the completed-square form and use the square-root sign for the stated domain.

Choose the positive square-root offset relative to \(3\).

Final answer: \(\sqrt{\frac{x}{2} - \frac{1}{2}} + 3\).

examples.title: Invert a quadratic on a single branch
examples.question:
The function \(f(x)=2 \left(x - 4\right)^{2} - 4\) has domain \(x\le 4\).

Find \(f^{-1}(-2)\).
examples.solution:
Solve the quadratic for the input and then keep the stated branch.

The equation gives \(5\) and \(3\). Keep the one that meets \(x\le 4\).

Final answer: \(3\).

lessons.title: Inverse graphs and fixed points
lessons.summary: Swap coordinates, reflect graphs across the diagonal and identify shared points.
lessons.objective: Swap coordinates, reflect graphs across the diagonal and identify shared points.
lessons.before: For each plotted point, the first coordinate becomes the second coordinate and the second becomes the first.
lessons.ideas:
A reflection in \(y=x\) swaps the two coordinates.

For the non-parallel lines here, solve \(f(x)=x\) to get the common point.

The horizontal intercept of the original becomes a vertical intercept of the inverse.
lessons.method:
Where does a point move on an inverse graph?

For each plotted point, the first coordinate becomes the second coordinate and the second becomes the first.

Where can these two lines meet?

A line and its distinct inverse are mirror images. Their unique intersection must be on the mirror line.

Which intercepts are exchanged?

An original point on the horizontal axis has output zero. Its inverse has input zero.
mistakes: The graph is reflected across the diagonal rather than across an axis.
Do not apply this single-intersection argument to arbitrary curves.
Keep the sign of the coordinate when swapping the axes.

examples.title: Use the diagonal reflection of an inverse
examples.question:
The graph of \(f(x)=3 x + 1\) contains the point \((2,7)\). Its inverse is defined for all real inputs.

Give the corresponding point on the inverse graph.
examples.solution:
Exchange the input and the output.

Reflection in \(y=x\) changes \((2,7)\) into \((7,2)\)

Final answer: \((7,2)\).

examples.title: Use the diagonal reflection of an inverse
examples.question:
The graph of \(f(x)=3 x + 2\) contains the point \((6,20)\). Its inverse is defined for all real inputs.

Find the intersection of the line and its inverse.
examples.solution:
Set the two line expressions equal. The common point is on the reflection line.

Use \(3 x + 2=x\) to find the fixed input \(-1\) and substitute it back.

Final answer: \((-1,-1)\).

examples.title: Use the diagonal reflection of an inverse
examples.question:
The graph of \(f(x)=3 x + 3\) contains the point \((3,12)\). Its inverse is defined for all real inputs.

Find the y-intercept of the inverse graph.
examples.solution:
The original x-intercept becomes the inverse y-intercept.

Solve \(3 x + 3=0\), then exchange coordinates.

Final answer: \(-1\).

questions.title: Find and use an inverse function
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(f(x)=-2 + \frac{5}{x - 12}\), \(x\ne 12\).

Give the value excluded from the domain of the inverse.
questions.solution_html:
Isolate the reciprocal term before switching the variable names.

From \(y=-2 + \frac{5}{x - 12}\), multiply by \(x-12\) and divide by \(y-(-2)\). The inverse excludes the original range gap. The inverse is \(f^{-1}(x)=12 + \frac{5}{x + 2}\).

questions.solution_html:

Isolate the reciprocal term before switching the variable names.

From \(y=-2 + \frac{3}{x - 26}\), multiply by \(x-26\) and divide by \(y-(-2)\). The inverse excludes the original range gap. The inverse is \(f^{-1}(x)=26 + \frac{3}{x + 2}\).

Find the input that the original function sends to the given output.

Substitution confirms \(f(27)=1\).

Final answer: \(27\).
